newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Thousands of rebels vote in Philippine polls.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of rebels vote in Philippine polls.

text.p: Ali Macabalang
Thousands of Moslem guerrillas laid down their weapons on Monday and voted to elect their chief, Nur Misuari, as regional governor of a semi-autonomous region in the southern Philippines.

Misuari, a former university professor who plunged the Mindanao region into 24 years of bloody civil war, cast his vote in a school house in his home town in Jolo and said it signalled the rebels' return to the political mainstream.
"This vote symbolises our commitment to peace, democracy and progress for our people here in Mindanao and eventually for the entire country," he said.
The chairman of the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) signed a peace deal with the government last week, ending a separatist war that killed more than 120,000 people.

Running unopposed, he needs one vote -- his or that of one of his two wives -- to win the governorship of a semi-autonomous region comprising four Moslem provinces. The area is considered to be among the poorest in the country.
Misuari is expected to be proclaimed the winner on Wednesday after the official count, the election commission said.

More than 2,000 rebels, many of them wearing battle fatigues and without their guns, voted in Maguindanao province in the first hours of polling. Thousands more cast their votes in the other areas, officials said.
"We did not bring our firearms because we are under the peace process," said MNLF district commander Basir Naim, one of more than 500 guerrillas who voted in Saguarian town.
Voting around the region was peaceful, police said.
But official poll watchers reported cases of cheating in some areas in Lanao del Sur, where two or three people, some of them rebels, voted for an entire district.
President Fidel Ramos said he expected Mindanao's economy to now take off.
"The era of peace that Mindanao will now enjoy offers a unique opportunity for the region...to emerge from the economic backwaters to the front door of progress," Ramos said in Manila.
Also at stake in the polls are the post of vice governor and all the seats of a 21-member regional legislative assembly.
Under his peace deal with Manila, Misuari will also head a Southern Philippine Council for Peace and Development to supervise the development of 14 provinces.
The council, bitterly opposed by some Christians, is seen as the precursor of a much wider autonomous regional government covering provinces that will vote to join it in a plebiscite.

Many Christians fear the deal could lead to MNLF political ascendancy in the region, which Moslems regard as their ancestral homeland but which Christian settlers now dominate by a three-to-one ratio.
Christian vigilante groups have been formed to oppose the pact by violence, but military officials dismiss them as insignificant.
Catholic Monsignor Crisanto de la Cruz, in a prayer rally attended by 1,500 people in Zamboanga city, accused Ramos of ignoring Christain demands.
"He knows that this kind of medicine he is giving us will not give us peace... Let us not gamble with peace. It is a very dangerous game," he said.
